questions.q: For theta = pi/2 and phi = 0 (the |+> state), what are the computed Bloch coordinates (x, y, z)?
questions.explain: x = sin(pi/2)*cos(0) = 1, y = sin(pi/2)*sin(0) = 0, z = cos(pi/2) = 0, placing the |+> state at (1, 0, 0) on the equator.

questions.q: Why does the Bloch sphere need two angles (theta and phi) instead of just one, given that a single qubit only has two possible measurement outcomes?
options: theta encodes the probability split between |0> and |1>, while phi encodes the relative phase between the amplitudes -- information a plain probability bar chart cannot show at all
Two angles are used purely for historical convention and carry no distinct physical meaning
theta and phi both encode the same probability information redundantly, as a cross-check
phi is only needed when more than one qubit is involved
questions.explain: P(0) and P(1) depend only on theta; phi captures the relative phase, which is invisible to measurement probabilities alone but changes the state's point on the Bloch sphere.

questions.q: Given amplitudes alpha = 1/sqrt(2) and beta = i/sqrt(2) (both contributing equally to probability, but beta purely imaginary), what Bloch coordinates does the direct amplitude formula (z = |alpha|^2 - |beta|^2, x = 2*Re(alpha*conj(beta)), y = 2*Im(conj(alpha)*beta)) produce?
questions.explain: z = 0.5 - 0.5 = 0; the real part of alpha*conj(beta) works out to 0 so x = 0; the imaginary part of conj(alpha)*beta works out to 0.5 so y = 2*0.5 = 1, giving (0, 1, 0), the |+i> state.

questions.q: In the mplot3d sphere-drawing code, what is the specific purpose of calling `ax.set_box_aspect([1, 1, 1])`?
options: It forces equal scaling on all three axes so the sphere renders as a true sphere instead of being stretched into an egg shape by Matplotlib's default 3D auto-scaling
It sets the sphere's radius to exactly 1 unit, which it would otherwise default to 2
It is required to enable the 3D projection in the first place, replacing the Axes3D import
It controls the color of the wireframe mesh lines
questions.explain: Matplotlib's default 3D axes don't automatically use equal scaling on x, y, and z; set_box_aspect([1,1,1]) forces that equal scaling so a geometrically round sphere doesn't appear stretched.

questions.q: When drawing the state vector with `ax.quiver(0, 0, 0, x, y, z, ...)`, why are the last three arguments simply the state's Bloch coordinates (x, y, z) rather than some other computed value?
options: `ax.quiver` draws an arrow as a displacement from the given start point, and since the arrow starts at the origin (0, 0, 0), the displacement to reach the point (x, y, z) is just (x, y, z) itself
quiver always draws arrows from the current point to the sphere's center, regardless of the arguments given
The last three arguments set the arrow's color, not its direction or length
x, y, z must first be divided by 2 to account for quiver's internal unit scaling
questions.explain: quiver's signature is (x0, y0, z0, dx, dy, dz): a start point plus a displacement. Starting at the origin, the displacement needed to reach (x, y, z) is exactly (x, y, z).
